pros: Handles negative edge weights (unlike running Dijkstra alone)
Faster than Floyd-Warshall for sparse graphs (E << V²)
More efficient than V runs of Bellman-Ford
Detects negative cycles early in the Bellman-Ford phase
Reweighting technique is elegant and theoretically sound
Uses efficient Dijkstra for the most expensive phase
Preserves all shortest path properties after reweighting
Well-suited for moderately sparse directed graphs
Potential function has independent mathematical interest
Parallelizable: each Dijkstra run is independent
cons: More complex to implement than Floyd-Warshall
Requires O(V²) memory to store all-pairs distances
Overhead of Bellman-Ford phase even for non-negative graphs
Not suitable for dense graphs (use Floyd-Warshall)
Cannot handle negative cycles (no algorithm can for paths)
Reweighting may cause numerical precision issues
Adding dummy node modifies graph structure temporarily
Dijkstra with binary heap may not be optimal for all graphs
Performance degrades with increasing graph density
Requires graph to be stored in memory (not external-memory friendly)
Implementation bugs in reweighting can be hard to detect
